blocks.html:
EXPOSÉ XXV
THE EXISTENCE THEOREMby M. Demazure

For the sake of completeness, we give in this exposé a proof of the existence theorem for split groups. Like Chevalley's original proof ("Sur certains schémas de groupes semi-simples", Séminaire Bourbaki, May 1961, no. 219), it rests on the existence of complex semi-simple algebraic groups of every possible type. The principle of a more satisfactory proof, establishing directly the existence of a simply connected split semi-simple \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group corresponding to a given Cartan matrix, has been given by Cartier (unpublished). Let us point out, however, that the difficulty is not to give an explicit construction of a group scheme, but to check that the group so constructed does indeed satisfy the required conditions, that is to say essentially that its fibres are smooth and reductive.
1. Statement of the theorem

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.1

Let S be a non-empty prescheme. The functor \[ G \longmapsto \mathrm{R}(G) \] is an equivalence of the category of pinned reductive S-group schemes with the category of pinned reduced root data.
By virtue of the uniqueness theorem (Exp. XXIII, 4.1), the preceding statement is equivalent to:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.2 (Existence of split groups)

For every reduced root datum \(\mathrm{R}\), there exists a split reductive \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group G such that \(\mathrm{R}(G) \simeq \mathrm{R}\).
In particular:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.3

Let \(k\) be a field. For every splittable reductive \(k\)-group \(G_k\), there exists a reductive \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group G such that \(G \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k \simeq G_k\).

Conversely, let us first remark that in order to prove 1.2, it suffices, by Exp. XXII, 4.3.1, Exp. XXI, 6.5.10, and the uniqueness theorem, to consider the case where the root datum \(\mathrm{R}\) is simply connected (and even irreducible if one insists, by Exp. XXI, 7.1.6). On the other hand, under the conditions of 1.3, the group scheme G is of constant type (since \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\) is connected), hence of type \(\mathrm{R}(G_k)\); by Exp. XXIII, 5.9, it follows that the validity of 1.3 for a given group \(G_k\) entails the existence of a split \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group of type \(\mathrm{R}(G_k)\).

In order to prove 1.2, and hence 1.1, it therefore suffices to prove 1.3 when \(k\) is of characteristic zero (for example \(k = \mathbb{C}\)) and \(G_k\) is simply connected (and in particular semi-simple), as well as:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.4

For every simply connected reduced root datum \(\mathrm{R}\), there exists a semi-simple algebraic \(\mathbb{C}\)-group of type \(\mathrm{R}\).

One can prove 1.4 in the following way. One knows first (cf. for example, Jacobson, Lie Algebras, ch. VII, Theorem 5) that there exists a complex semi-simple Lie algebra of type \(\mathrm{R}\). Taking the identity component of the group of automorphisms of this algebra, one obtains a semi-simple algebraic \(\mathbb{C}\)-group of type \(\mathrm{ad}(\mathrm{R})\). By BIBLE, 23-01, prop. 1, one deduces from this the existence of a group of type \(\mathrm{R}\).

The remainder of this exposé is devoted to the proof of 1.3 for \(k\) of characteristic zero and \(G_k\) semi-simple. It will be carried out in two stages: construction of a "piece of a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group prescheme" (no. 2), study of the group obtained by application of the "Weil theorem" (no. 3).
To avoid confusion, we shall not use in no. 2 the abbreviated notation \(X_k\) to denote the \(k\)-prescheme \(X \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\), where \(X\) is a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-prescheme.

pages.title: 2. The existence theorem: construction of a piece of a group

blocks.html: 2. The existence theorem: construction of a piece of a group

Let us choose once and for all a splitting of \(G_k\), denoted \[ (G_k, T_k, M, R) \] (cf. Exp. XXII, 1.13), a system of simple roots \(R_0\) of \(R\) (defining the system of positive roots \(R^+\)), a Chevalley system \((X_{\alpha, k})_{\alpha \in R}\) of \(G_k\) (Exp. XXIII, 6.1 and 6.2) satisfying the following supplementary condition: if \(\alpha \in R\), one has \(X_{\alpha,k} X_{-\alpha,k} = 1\). Let us finally choose on the subgroup of \(M\) generated by \(R\) a total order relation compatible with the group structure, such that the roots \(> 0\) are the elements of \(R^+\). We shall then denote the roots by \[ -\alpha_n < -\alpha_{n-1} < \cdots < -\alpha_1 < \alpha_1 < \alpha_2 < \cdots < \alpha_n. \]

For \(\alpha \in R\), we shall denote by \(U_{\alpha, k}\) the vector group corresponding to the root \(\alpha\) and by \[ p_{\alpha,k} : \mathbb{G}_{a, k} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} U_{\alpha, k} \] the isomorphism of vector groups defined by \(X_{\alpha, k}\).

The splitting of G comprises in particular an isomorphism of \(k\)-groups \[ T_k \simeq \mathbf{D}_k(M). \] Set \(T = \mathbf{D}(M)\); this is a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-torus, and one may regard the preceding isomorphism as an isomorphism \[ T_k \simeq T \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k. \] One has \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}\text{-gr.}}(T, \mathbb{G}_{m, S}) = M, \] and we shall regard the elements of \(R \subset M\) as characters of \(T\). We shall likewise regard the elements of \(R^*\) as morphisms of \(\mathbb{Z}\)-groups \(\mathbb{G}_m \to T\).

For each \(\alpha \in R^+\), let \(\mathbb{G}_a(\alpha)\) be a copy of the group \(\mathbb{G}_a\); consider the \(\mathbb{Z}\)-prescheme \[ U = \mathbb{G}_a(\alpha_1) \times \cdots \times \mathbb{G}_a(\alpha_n). \] If \(U_k\) denotes the unipotent part of the Borel group \(B_k\) of \(G_k\) defined by \(R^+\), let us denote by \[ a : U \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} U_k \] the isomorphism of \(k\)-preschemes defined by \[ a((x_i)) = p_{\alpha_1, k}(x_1) \cdots p_{\alpha_n, k}(x_n). \]

The group law of \(U_k\) translates into relations of the form \[ a((x_i)) \cdot a((y_j)) = a((z_h)), \] where each \(z_h\) is expressed as a polynomial \[ z_h = x_h + y_h + Q_h(x_1, \ldots, x_{h-1}, y_1, \ldots, y_{h-1}), \] the coefficients of \(Q_h\) being integers (Exp. XXII, 5.5.8 and Exp. XXIII, 6.4). Moreover \(Q_h(x_1, \ldots, x_{h-1}, 0, \ldots, 0) = 0\).

Let us equip \(U\) with the composition law defined by the preceding formulas (which are indeed "defined over \(\mathbb{Z}\)"). Since this law induces on \(U_k\) its group law, it is associative, and \((0)\) is a unit element for it (indeed, the two preceding assertions are expressed by relations between the polynomials \(Q_h\), and \(\mathbb{Z} \to k\) is injective). Let us show that it is a group law: if \((x_i)\) is a section of \(U\) (over an arbitrary S), one computes the inverse \((y_i)\) of \((x_i)\) by the recurrence formulas \[ y_i = -x_i - Q_i(x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}) \] which are again "defined over \(\mathbb{Z}\)".
To sum up, we have constructed on \(U\) a group law such that the preceding isomorphism \(a\) is an isomorphism of groups.

For each \(\alpha \in R^+\), consider the morphism \[ p_\alpha : \mathbb{G}_a \longrightarrow U \] defined by \(p_\alpha(x) = (x_i)\) where \[ x_i = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } \alpha_i = \alpha \\ 0 & \text{if } \alpha_i \neq \alpha. \end{cases} \]

It is a closed immersion and a homomorphism of groups; we shall denote by \(U_\alpha\) its image. One has \((x_i) = p_{\alpha_1}(x_1) \cdots p_{\alpha_n}(x_n)\), which proves that \(U\) is identified with the product \[ U = U_{\alpha_1} \cdot U_{\alpha_2} \cdots U_{\alpha_n}. \]

Let us make \(T = \mathbf{D}(M)\) operate on each \(U_\alpha\) by means of the character \(\alpha\); one checks at once that this defines an operation of \(T\) on the group \(U\), and one can construct the semi-direct product \(B = T \cdot U\). One has a canonical isomorphism of \(k\)-groups \[ B \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} B_k. \]

If we now take an arbitrary order on \(R^+\), the morphism \[ \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} U_\alpha \longrightarrow U \] defined by the product in \(U\) is still an isomorphism. Indeed, since both sides are flat \(\mathbb{Z}\)-preschemes of finite presentation, it is enough to check the assertion on the geometric fibres; one is then reduced to Lazard's theory (BIBLE, § 13.1, prop. 1): one regards \(U\) as a group with operators \(T\), and one uses the fact that the \(U_\alpha\) are pairwise non-isomorphic as groups with operators (since the characters \(\alpha \in R^+\) of \(T\) are pairwise distinct on each fibre).

Replacing \(R^+\) by \(R^- = -R^+\), one constructs in the same way groups \(U^-\), \(B^-\), \(U_\alpha\) (\(\alpha \in R^-\)) and isomorphisms \[ p_\alpha : \mathbb{G}_a \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} U_\alpha, \qquad \alpha \in R^-. \] Let us finally introduce the product prescheme \[ \Omega = U^- \times T \times U\,; \] one has a canonical isomorphism of \(k\)-preschemes \[ \Omega \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} U_k^- \times_k T_k \times_k U_k \simeq \Omega_k, \] where \(\Omega_k\) is the "big cell" of \(G_k\) (Exp. XXII, 4.1.2).

From now on, we shall identify \(\Omega \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) with \(\Omega_k\) by the preceding isomorphism; we shall regard \(U^-\), \(T\), \(U\) as sub-preschemes of \(\Omega\), by means of the unit sections. We shall denote by \(e = ((0), e, (0))\) the "unit section" of \(\Omega\).
Our aim is now to put a law of a piece of a group on \(\Omega\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.7

Let \(\alpha \in R_0\), and let \(w_{\alpha, k}\) be the element of \(\mathrm{Norm}_{G_k}(T_k)(k)\) defined by \(X_{\alpha, k}\) (recall that one has by definition \[ w_{\alpha,k} = p_{-\alpha,k}(-1) \, p_{\alpha,k}(1) \, p_{-\alpha,k}(-1)\text{).} \] There exist an open subset \(V_\alpha\) of \(\Omega\), containing the section \(e\), and a morphism \[ h_\alpha : V_\alpha \longrightarrow \Omega, \] satisfying the following conditions:

(i) \(h_\alpha(e) = e\),

(ii) \((h_\alpha) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) coincides with the restriction of \(\mathrm{int}(w_{\alpha,k})\) to \(V_\alpha \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k \subset G_k\).

(iii) One has \(T \subset V_\alpha\) and \(h_\alpha\) sends \(T\) into \(T\). For every \(\beta \in R\), one has \(U_\beta \subset V_\alpha\) and \(h_\alpha\) sends \(U_\beta\) into \(U_{s_\alpha(\beta)}\).

By virtue of the definition of a Chevalley system (Exp. XXIII, 6.1), there exists for each \(\beta \in R\) an integer \(e_\beta = \pm 1\) such that \[ \mathrm{int}(w_{\alpha,k}) \, p_{\beta, k}(x) = p_{s_\alpha(\beta), k}(e_\beta x) \] for every \(x \in \mathbb{G}_a(S)\), \(S \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\).

Let \(S\) be an arbitrary prescheme; let us write an arbitrary element of \(\Omega(S)\) in the form \[ n = \Bigl(\prod_{\substack{\beta \in R^- \\ \beta \neq -\alpha}} p_\beta(x_\beta)\Bigr) \cdot p_{-\alpha}(x_{-\alpha}),\; t,\; p_\alpha(x_\alpha) \cdot \Bigl(\prod_{\substack{\beta \in R^+ \\ \beta \neq \alpha}} p_\beta(x_\beta)\Bigr), \] where one has chosen an (arbitrary) order on \(R^- - \{-\alpha\}\) and \(R^+ - \{\alpha\}\) (cf. 2.5).
One defines a morphism \(d : \Omega \to \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\) by \[ d(u) = \alpha(t) + x_\alpha x_{-\alpha}. \]

Let \(V_\alpha\) be the open subset \(\Omega_d\) (that is to say the open subset of \(\Omega\) defined by "\(d(u)\) invertible"); it contains \(e\), \(T\), and each \(U_\beta\), \(\beta \in R\). Let \[ h_\alpha : V_\alpha \longrightarrow \Omega \] be the morphism defined by \(h_\alpha(u) = (a(u), b(u), c(u))\) where \[ a(u) = \Bigl(\prod_{\substack{\beta \in R^- \\ \beta \neq -\alpha}} p_{s_\alpha(\beta)}(e_\beta x_\beta)\Bigr) \cdot p_{-\alpha}\bigl(-x_\alpha \, d(u)^{-1}\bigr) \] \[ b(u) = t \cdot \alpha^*(d(u)), \] \[ c(u) = p_\alpha\bigl(-x_{-\alpha} \, d(u)^{-1}\bigr) \cdot \Bigl(\prod_{\substack{\beta \in R^+ \\ \beta \neq \alpha}} p_{s_\alpha(\beta)}(e_\beta x_\beta)\Bigr). \]

Since \(s_\alpha\) permutes the positive (resp. negative) roots distinct from \(\alpha\) (resp. \(-\alpha\)), \(c(u)\) (resp. \(a(u)\)) is a section of \(U\) (resp. \(U^-\)) and the preceding morphism is well defined. It trivially satisfies (i) and (iii). As for (ii), this follows at once from the definition of the \(e_\beta\), \(\beta \in R\), and from Exp. XX, 3.12.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.8

There exist open subsets \(V\) and \(V'\) of \(\Omega\) and morphisms \[ h : V \longrightarrow \Omega, \] \[ h' : V' \longrightarrow \Omega, \] satisfying the following conditions:

(i) \(V\) and \(V'\) contain \(e\), and \(h(e) = h'(e) = e\).

(ii) The morphism induced by \(h' \circ h : h^{-1}(V') \to \Omega\) is the restriction of the identity morphism.

(iii) The \(k\)-morphisms \(h \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) and \(h' \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) are the restriction to \(V \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) and \(V' \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) of automorphisms of the group \(G_k\).

(iv) \(V\) and \(V'\) contain \(U\), \(T\) and \(U^-\); \(h\) and \(h'\) send \(U\) into \(U^-\), \(U^-\) into \(U\), and \(T\) into \(T\).

Let \(w_0\) be the element of the Weyl group of \(G_k\) which transforms \(R^+\) into \(R^-\). Let us write \[ w_0 = s_{\alpha_n} \cdots s_{\alpha_1}, \qquad \alpha_i \in R_0 \] (no connection with the numbering of 2.1). Set \[ w_0 = w_{\alpha_n, k} \cdots w_{\alpha_1, k} \in \mathrm{Norm}_{G_k}(T_k)(k). \] Let us define by induction on \(i \leqslant n\) an open subset \(V_i\) of \(\Omega\) and a morphism \(h_i : V_i \to \Omega\) by \[ V_0 = \Omega, \quad h_0 = \mathrm{id}, \] \[ V_{i+1} = h_i^{-1}(V_{\alpha_{i+1}}), \quad h_{i+1} = h_{\alpha_{i+1}} \circ h_i, \quad 0 \leqslant i < n \] (the notations \(V_\alpha\), \(h_\alpha\) are those of 2.7).

Let us take \(V = V_n\) and \(h = h_n\). The conditions of (i), (iii) and (iv) bearing on \(V\) and \(h\) are indeed satisfied; for (i) and (iii) this follows at once from 2.8, for (iv), from the fact that \(h \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) is the restriction of \(\mathrm{int}(w_0)\) to \(V \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\).
Since \((w_0)^2 = 1\), one also has \[ w_0 = s_{\alpha_1} \cdots s_{\alpha_n} = (s_{\alpha_1}^3) \cdots (s_{\alpha_n}^3). \]

Setting \[ w_0' = (w_{\alpha_1, k})^3 \cdots (w_{\alpha_n, k})^3, \] and carrying out the same construction as above, one deduces from this an open subset \(V'\) and a morphism \(h'\) also satisfying (i), (iii), (iv). Moreover, \(h' \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) is the restriction of \(\mathrm{int}(w_0')\) to \(V' \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\). But for each simple root \(\alpha \in R_0\), one has \((w_{\alpha, k})^4 = e\) (cf. Exp. XX, 3.1), hence \(w_0' \cdot w_0 = e\), which shows that \(h' \circ h\) induces the identity morphism on a non-empty open subset of \(\Omega \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\). But \(\Omega\) being smooth and of finite presentation over \(\mathbb{Z}\), \(\Omega \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) is schematically dense in \(\Omega\), which proves (ii).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.9

There exist an open subset \(V_1\) of \(\Omega \times \Omega\), an open subset \(V_2\) of \(\Omega\), and morphisms \[ \pi : V_1 \longrightarrow \Omega, \qquad \sigma : V_2 \longrightarrow \Omega, \] possessing the following properties:

(i) If \(x \in \Omega(S)\), then \((e, x)\) (resp. \((x, e)\)) is a section of \(V_1\) and \(\pi(e, x) = \pi(x, e) = x\).

(ii) \(V_2\) contains \(e\) and \(\sigma(e) = e\).

(iii) \(\pi_k\) and \(\sigma_k\) are the restriction of the morphisms \(G_k \times_k G_k \to G_k\) and \(G_k \to G_k\) defined by the product (resp. the inverse).

Proof. — Let \((v, t, u)\) and \((v', t', u')\) be two sections of \(\Omega\). Then \(h(u)\) is a section of \(U^-\), \(h(v')\) is a section of \(U\) by 2.8 (iv), and one may therefore regard \((h(u), e, h(v'))\) as a section of \(\Omega\). Let \(V_1\) be the open subset of \(\Omega \times \Omega\) defined by the condition: \[ \bigl((v, t, u),\, (v', t', u')\bigr) \in V_1(S) \iff (h(u), e, h(v')) \in V'(S) \] (notations of 2.8). If \(\bigl((v, t, u),\, (v', t', u')\bigr)\) is a section of \(V_1\), then \(h'(h(u), e, h(v'))\) is defined; it is a section of \(\Omega\) which one may decompose: \[ h'(h(u), e, h(v')) = (v'', t'', u''). \] One will then set \[ \pi\bigl((v, t, u),\, (v', t', u')\bigr) = (v \cdot t v'' t^{-1},\; t t'' t',\; t'^{-1} u'' t' \cdot u'). \]

The verification of (i) is immediate (by 2.8 (ii)). To verify the condition of (iii) bearing on \(\pi\), one sees that \[ h'(h(u), e, h(v')) = u v' = v'' t'' u'' \] when \(u \in U(S)\), \(v \in U^-(S)\), \(S \to k\), by virtue of 2.8 (iii) and (ii). One constructs \(\sigma\) in a similar manner: if \((v, t, u)\) is a section of \(\Omega\), \(h(u^{-1})\) is a section of \(U^-\), \(h(v^{-1})\) a section of \(U\), \(h(t^{-1})\) a section of \(T\), hence \((h(u^{-1}), h(t^{-1}), h(v^{-1}))\) is a section of \(\Omega\) and one may define an open subset \(V_2\) of \(\Omega\) by \[ (v, t, u) \in V_2(S) \iff (h(u^{-1}), h(t^{-1}), h(v^{-1})) \in V'(S) \] and a morphism \(\sigma : V_2 \to \Omega\) by \[ \sigma(v, t, u) = h'(h(u^{-1}), h(t^{-1}), h(v^{-1})). \] One verifies the conditions on \(\sigma\) as above.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.10

\(\pi\) is "generically associative" and \(\sigma\) is a "generic inverse": if \(x, y, z \in \Omega(S)\) and if the expressions below are defined (which always happens over an open subset of \(\Omega\) containing the unit section), one has: \[ \pi(x, \pi(y, z)) = \pi(\pi(x, y), z), \] \[ \pi(x, \sigma(x)) = e = \pi(\sigma(x), x). \]
Indeed, the two sides of each of these formulas define morphisms between smooth \(\mathbb{Z}\)-preschemes of finite presentation, which coincide on the generic fibres, by 2.10 (iii).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.11

Let \(\alpha \in R\). For every S and all \(x, y \in \mathbb{G}_a(S)\) such that \((p_\alpha(x), p_{-\alpha}(y)) \in V_1(S)\) and \(1 + xy \in \mathbb{G}_m(S)\) (which defines an open subset of \(\mathbb{G}_{a,S}^2\) containing the section \((0, 0)\)), one has: \[ \pi(p_\alpha(x),\, p_{-\alpha}(y)) = \Bigl(p_{-\alpha}\Bigl(\frac{y}{1+xy}\Bigr),\; \alpha^*(1+xy),\; p_\alpha\Bigl(\frac{x}{1+xy}\Bigr)\Bigr). \]
The proof is the same as before, by Exp. XX, 2.1.

pages.title: 3. The existence theorem: end of the proof

blocks.html: 3. The existence theorem: end of the proof
To simplify the language, let us lay down the following definition.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.1

Let S be a prescheme and G an S-group prescheme. One says that G is admissible if there exists an open immersion of S-preschemes \(i : \Omega_S = \Omega \times S \to G\) satisfying the following conditions:

  1. (i)

    The diagram \[ \xymatrix{ (V_1)_S \ar[r]^-{i \times_S i} \ar[d]_{\pi} & \Omega_S \times_S \Omega_S \ar[r] & G \times_S G \ar[d]^{\pi_G} \\ \Omega_S \ar[rr]^-{i_S} & & G, } \] where \(\pi_G\) denotes the multiplication morphism in G, is commutative.

  2. (ii)

    There exists a finite set of sections \(a_j \in \Omega(S)\) such that the \(i(a_j) \cdot i(\Omega_S)\) cover G.
By the "Weil theorem" (Exp. XVIII, 3.13 (iii) and (iv)), one has:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.2

If for every prescheme S étale and of finite type over \(\mathbb{Z}\), every admissible S-group is affine, then there exists an admissible and affine \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group.
Now one has:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.3

Let S be a prescheme and G an admissible S-group. Then G is smooth and of finite presentation over S, with connected semi-simple affine fibres.

Since \(\Omega_S\) is smooth and of finite presentation over S, with connected fibres, the same holds for G, by virtue of condition (ii). To verify 3.3, one may therefore assume that S is the spectrum of a field K. Let us identify \(\Omega_K\) with its image in G. It is clear that \(\Omega_K\) is the product \[ \prod_{\alpha \in R^-} U_{\alpha, K} \cdot T_K \cdot \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} U_{\alpha, K} \] of the subgroups \(T_K\) and \(U_{\alpha, K}\) (\(\alpha \in R\)) of G. The Lie algebra of G is therefore identified with the direct sum \[ \mathrm{Lie}(T_K) \bigoplus_{\alpha \in R} \mathrm{Lie}(U_{\alpha, K}). \]

Since the inner automorphism defined by a section of \(T_K\) operates in \(U_{\alpha, K}\), and hence in \(\mathrm{Lie}(U_{\alpha, K})\), by means of the character \[ \alpha \in R \subset M \simeq \mathrm{Hom}_{K\text{-gr.}}(T_K, \mathbb{G}_{m, K}), \] the preceding decomposition of \(\mathrm{Lie}(G)\) is exactly the decomposition under the adjoint operation of T. The roots of \(G_K\) relative to \(T_K\) are therefore the \(\alpha \in R\). Let us apply Exp. XIX, 1.13. Let \(T_\alpha\) be the maximal torus of \(\mathrm{Ker}(\alpha) \subset T_K\) and let

\(Z_\alpha = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(T_\alpha)\); it suffices for us to prove that each \(Z_\alpha\) is reductive. Now \(Z_\alpha \cap \Omega_K\) is none other than \[ \prod_{\substack{\beta \in R^- \\ \beta|_{T_\alpha} = e}} U_{\beta, K} \cdot T_K \cdot \prod_{\substack{\beta \in R^+ \\ \beta|_{T_\alpha} = e}} U_{\beta, K}\,; \] but the roots vanishing on \(T_\alpha\) are the rational multiples of \(\alpha\), hence \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\); which proves \[ Z_\alpha \cap \Omega_K = U_{-\alpha, K} \cdot T_K \cdot U_{\alpha, K}. \] To prove that \(Z_\alpha\) is reductive it suffices, by virtue of Exp. XX 3.4, to prove that \(U_{\alpha, K}\) and \(U_{-\alpha, K}\) do not commute, which follows at once from 2.11.
It follows from 3.2 and 3.3 that the proof will be complete if we prove:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.4

If S is a locally noetherian prescheme of dimension \(\leqslant 1\), and if G is a smooth S-group of finite type, with connected semi-simple affine fibres, then G is affine (and hence semi-simple).
Nota. — In Exp. XVI, it was seen that 3.4 is true without any hypothesis on S, but the proof is relatively delicate; since here we need only the special case 3.4, we shall give a direct proof of it.

Let us consider the Lie Algebra \(\mathfrak{g}\) of G, which is a locally free \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-module, and the adjoint representation of G \[ \mathrm{Ad} : G \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{GL}}_{\mathscr{O}_S}(\mathfrak{g}). \]

To prove that G is affine over S, it suffices to prove that the morphism Ad is affine. Since G is smooth and has connected fibres, it is separated over S (Exp. VI), hence the morphism Ad is separated. Using a result proved in the appendix (see 4.1), it suffices to prove that the morphism Ad is quasi-finite. One is therefore reduced to the case where S is the spectrum of a field; in that case G is affine, hence semi-simple, and one is reduced to Exp. XXII 5.7.14.
4. Appendix
We have used in the course of the proof the following proposition:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.1

Let S be a locally noetherian prescheme of dimension \(\leqslant 1\), G and H two S-group preschemes of finite type, \(f : G \to H\) a quasi-finite and separated morphism of groups. Then \(f\) is affine.
We shall give the proof only in the case where G is smooth over S, a hypothesis which is indeed satisfied in the application we have made of the proposition.

By EGA II, 1.6.4, one may assume S reduced. By the usual techniques of passage to the limit, one may assume S local. If \(\dim(S) = 0\), the assertion is trivial; let us assume \(\dim(S) = 1\). By faithfully flat descent, one may even take S complete with algebraically closed residue field. After possibly normalising S, one may (EGA II, 6.7.1 and EGA \(0_{\mathrm{IV}}\) 23.1.5) assume S normal. One is therefore reduced to the case where S is the spectrum of a complete discrete valuation ring A with algebraically closed residue field.

Let \(\eta\) be the generic point of S. Let us consider the image \(f_\eta(G_\eta)\) of \(G_\eta\) in \(H_\eta\). It is a closed group subscheme of \(H_\eta\). Let \(H'\) be the schematic closure in H of \(f_\eta(G_\eta)\). Since \(H' \to H\) is affine (it is a closed immersion), one may replace H by \(H'\) and hence assume H flat over S and \(f_\eta\) surjective. Since \(f_\eta\) is finite, and G and H flat, one has \[ \dim(G_0) = \dim(G_\eta) = \dim(H_\eta) = \dim(H_0) \] (where the special fibres are denoted by an index "0").

Let \(H_0^{(0)}, \ldots, H_0^{(n)}\) be the irreducible components of \(H_0\), \(H_0^{(0)}\) denoting the identity component, and \(z_i\) their generic points. Since each local ring \(\mathscr{O}_{H, z_i}\) is of dimension \(\leqslant 1\), the morphism \(G \times_H \mathscr{O}_{H, z_i} \to \mathscr{O}_{H, z_i}\) is affine, being quasi-finite and separated (cf. lemma …, Exp. XVI), hence G is affine over H in a neighbourhood of \(z_i\). Denoting by V the largest open subset of H such that \(G|_V\) is affine over V, it follows that V contains all the \(z_i\).

On the other hand, V is obviously stable under the translation defined by an arbitrary element \(g \in G(S)\). But one has \(\dim(G_0) = \dim(H_0)\) and \(f_0\) is finite, hence \[ f_0 : G_0^{(0)}(s_0) \longrightarrow H_0^{(0)}(s_0) \] is surjective. Since A is complete and G smooth over S, the canonical map \(G^{(0)}(S) \to G_0^{(0)}(s_0)\) is surjective; one deduces from this that for every \(h_0 \in H_0^{(0)}(s_0)\), there exists a \(g \in G(S)\) such that \(f(g_0) = h_0\). Since \(H_0^{(0)}(s_0)\) operates transitively in each \(H_0^{(i)}(s_0)\), it follows that \(V \supset H_0(s_0)\), hence (\(k(s_0)\) being algebraically closed) \(V \supset H_0\).
Since one obviously has \(V \supset H_\eta\), \(f_\eta\) being finite, one has \(V = H\). Q.E.D.
